## What to do when GitHub flags a leaked secret When GitHub’s secret scanning tool (or a Dependabot alert) identifies a secret in your repo, it means someone (you or someone who cloned the repo) accidentally committed sensitive data—API keys, passwords, tokens, certificates, etc. The quickest way to mitigate risk is a **“chase‑down‑and‑rotate”** workflow: | Step | What to do | Why it matters | Quick tip | |------|------------|----------------|-----------| | **1. Identify the secret** | Click the alert link → “See secret” → note the exact string and hash. | You need to know *what* was leaked. | The alert gives a SHA‑256 hash of the secret; use `git log -S ` to locate the commit. | | **2. Find all commits containing it** | `git log -S '' --all` or use GitHub’s “Reveal secret” button. | A single commit might not be the only one. | On GitHub’s UI, “See all commits” can be auto‑generated. | | **3. Remove the secret from history** | *If the key is still in the public repo*
`git filter-branch --force --tree-filter 'git rm -f path/to/file' --prune-empty --tag-name-filter cat -- --all`
or use [BFG Repo-Cleaner](https://rtyley.github.io/bfg-repo-cleaner/) for speed. | Prevent anyone from pulling the repo and seeing the secret later. | **Back up first** (`git clone --mirror`). | | **4. Push the cleaned history** | `git push --force-with-lease` | Overwrite the bad history on GitHub. | Only do this if you’re the sole owner or if you have coordinated with collaborators. | | **5. Rotate the secret** | Immediately revoke or rotate the key/API token. | Even if the key is removed, it may still be valid. | If it’s a cloud service key (AWS, GCP, GitHub, etc.), update permissions—least‑privilege principle. | | **6. Inform your team** | Send a short safety notice: “We removed the leaked secret, rotated the key, and cleaned repo history.” | Keeps everyone in the loop, avoids duplicate scrapes. | Use a short FAQ: “No one was compromised… the key was rotated.” | | **7. (Optional) Re‑scan your repo** | After cleaning, let GitHub re‑run secret scanning or trigger it manually via the “Re‑scan” button. | Confirms removal. | Helps catch any remaining leaks. | | **8. Prevent future leaks** |
  • Set up pre‑commit hooks (`pre-commit`, `secrets` hook, etc.)
  • Use tools like GitGuardian, TruffleHog, or GitHub’s built‑in scanner for CI.
  • Store secrets in a dedicated vault (AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault, GitHub Secrets).
| Reduce human error. | Add the `no_commit` rule to your `.gitignore` for secret files. | ### A quick “compact” checklist 1. **See the alert → note the secret.** 2. **`git log -S '' --all` → find all occurrences.** 3. **Clean history** (`bfg`, or `git filter-branch`). 4. **Force‑push** (`git push --force-with-lease`). 5. **Rotate the credential** (API key, password, token, cert). 6. **Notify team + document the action.** 7. **Re‑run secret scan, confirm clean.** 8. **Set up preventive measures.** --- ## Common Pitfalls & How to Avoid Them | Pitfall | What to check | |---------|---------------| | **Leaving old tags** | Reset tags or force‑push them too: `git push --force -f origin ` | | **Cloned forks still contain the secret** | All forks must be cleaned too; contact maintainers. | | **Leaving the secret in a build artifact** | Check CI logs, build artifacts, Docker images, etc. | | **Not revoking the key** | Even if history is cleaned, the key can still be used. | | **Using the same key in multiple repos** | If unknown, search all repos (GitHub search, `grep` in local copies). | | **Force–pushing on a shared repo without coordination** | Can disrupt collaborators. Coordinate merge windows. | --- ## Extra Resources | Topic | Link | |-------|------| | GitHub Secret Scanning docs | https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/secret-scanning | | BFG Repo-Cleaner | https://rtyley.github.io/bfg-repo-cleaner/ | | GitHub Re‑scan a repo | https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/secret-scanning/scanning-your-repository-for-secrets#re-scanning-your-repository | | Pre‑commit secret detection | https://pre-commit.com/hooks/pre-commit-hooks.html#pre-commit-hooks-secret‑scan | | GitHub Actions secrets best practices | https://docs.github.com/en/actions/security-guides/security-hardening-for-github-actions | --- ### Quick “did‑i‑do‑everything?” check - ✅ All commits containing the secret were deleted or rewritten. - ✅ Push succeeded with `--force-with-lease`. - ✅ Key was rotated or revoked. - ✅ Re‑scan shows **no** remaining secrets. - ✅ Team is aware and updated on policy changes. If all of those are `✅`, you’re good to go! If something is still `❗`, revisit the steps—especially the cleanup and rotation steps. --- **Bottom line:** *Find, delete, rotate, inform, prevent.* Done.
